What more cases buy: inferential targets for reproduction-number estimates and what cross-sectional dispersion diagnostics measure

[Author names and affiliations to be added before submission]

4 November 2026

Abstract

Case counts often set the precision attributed to reproduction-number estimates, but the error that more cases remove depends on the inferential target. In a one-generation branching model with negative binomial offspring and binomial reporting, we derive exact mean squared errors for the current reproduction number, the realised mean over observed periods and the process mean. Counting error falls inversely with expected count for all three targets; the process mean also retains between-period transmission variance. Using the previous observed count as denominator raised the counting error 1.5-fold at large counts and 2.4-fold at ten expected cases under illustrative parameters. Under period-level reporting fluctuation, single-period count moments cannot separate reporting volatility from transmission variation. A simulation study on the design of 1,748 US state-weeks of influenza hospital admissions (2022–2025) assessed cross-sectional dispersion diagnostics against known truth. The intercept of an affine fit of relative squared deviation on inverse count recovered transmission variance under fixed reporting and the transmission-plus-reporting total under reporting shocks, and was smaller than transmission variance when heterogeneity scaled with count. The observed intercept was 0.0150 (95% CI 0.0109–0.0191 with a two-way cluster-robust sandwich and 0.0101–0.0206 with a conservative bootstrap). Read through the recovery ratios of the audited generators and share-grid cells, at the audited offspring dispersion and reporting probability, it corresponds to a transmission relative standard deviation of 6–19% (5–20% with the uncertainty in the intercept propagated). None of these mechanisms reproduced every tested summary, so the range is a conditional envelope and not an interval estimate. The counting slope was 1.26 (bootstrap 0.81–1.73) times the independent-Poisson reference and the dispersion-to-counting crossover 37 weekly admissions (sandwich 24–58; bootstrap 18–72). Evidence on differences between seasons was equivocal: a test of equal season intercepts gave p=0.064–0.22 in four uncalibrated specifications and calibrated p=0.005–0.045 against simulated null distributions whose panels carried less dependent variation than the data. Counting slopes and thinning did not distinguish overdispersion, under-reporting and heterogeneous transmission, whereas in-sample and held-out curve shapes weighed against heterogeneity that does not depend on count.

Keywords: reproduction number; surveillance; overdispersion; reporting variation; simulation study

1 Introduction

Reproduction numbers summarise transmission under specified conditions and are routinely estimated from surveillance counts [1, 2]. Renewal methods relate incidence to past infectiousness through a generation-interval distribution, and the width of their credible intervals shrinks as the number of cases grows [3, 4]. Work on low incidence, reporting noise and timely detection has made the limits of period-specific inference explicit [5–7], and temporal aggregation and reporting delays separate the reproduction number of the transmission process from the apparent reproduction number of an observed series [8–10].

Precision guidance for renewal estimators has been stated in cases. Cori et al. [3] tabulate the number of incident cases a time window needs for a chosen posterior coefficient of variation and recommend starting estimation once at least 12 cases have accrued. Under a gamma prior with shape a0, that coefficient is (a0+IW)−1/2, where IW is the number of cases in the window, so it is a function of the window count alone. It measures counting error for the average transmission level over the window. The estimate is also often read as the transmission level now or as a typical level for the population. For those targets, variation between periods is an additional error component that more cases do not remove. The criterion is therefore correct for one target and incomplete for the other two, and the distinction depends on which target the analyst intends.

The variance structure behind this distinction is classical. Variance-component models split the variance of a unit-level estimate into a within-unit sampling term and a between-unit term [11, 12]. Random-effects meta-analysis estimates the between-study component on top of within-study error [13], and small-area estimation and empirical-Bayes disease mapping weight each direct estimate against a common mean according to the ratio of the two terms [14–16]. Funnel plots for institutional comparison draw control limits from the counting term and add an overdispersion component when units differ beyond chance [17]. Population ecology makes the same split between demographic and environmental stochasticity [18, 19], as do stochastic epidemic models [20, 21]. In each setting the count at which the two terms are equal is where a shrinkage estimator places half its weight on the direct estimate.

Several results used below are standard and are cited where they are applied. The mean squared error decompositions follow from the law of total variance [11, 22]. The efficiency of the count-to-scale ratio for a Poisson mean is the Cramér–Rao bound [23], the delta-method expansion of a ratio estimator is textbook material [22], and the square-root allocation of surveillance effort is Neyman allocation [12]. Offspring overdispersion follows Lloyd-Smith et al. [24], and its estimation from small samples Lloyd-Smith [25]. A variance that scales as a power of the mean is Taylor’s law [26], the alternative to the affine form that Section 4 tests. The distinction between the realised quantity of a finite population and the parameter of the process that generated it follows Graubard and Korn [27].

The paper makes four contributions. Section 2 sets out three inferential targets for a period-specific reproduction number and derives their exact mean squared errors in a branching model with negative binomial offspring and binomial reporting, together with the correction required when the denominator is the previous observed count. Section 3 shows that, when the reporting probability fluctuates between periods, single-period second moments of the counts cannot separate reporting volatility from transmission variation, and that the realised-mean target then retains a reporting term. Section 4 defines three cross-sectional dispersion diagnostics for surveillance counts, with reference values for the counting slope under independent Poisson and branching Poisson counting. The same section reports a known-truth simulation study on the real sampling design, including a grid over the share of variance carried by transmission, the coverage of dependence-aware intervals and simulated reference distributions for the season and held-out comparisons. Section 5 applies the diagnostics to 1,748 state-weeks of US influenza hospital admissions.

The diagnostics address a practical gap. Routine hospital surveillance does not observe the variables of a branching experiment. Admissions follow infection after a delay, aggregate heterogeneous populations and are recorded on a calendar schedule, and their count scale is an outcome of the epidemic. Reporting probabilities may change for all infections in the same period [28, 29], and separating process from observation variation in time series is a known difficulty [30, 31]. The cross-sectional spread of growth-rate or reproduction-number estimates has been read as variation in transmission or behaviour between places and periods without subtracting the part of that spread that depends on case counts [32, 33], although per-unit standard errors make the subtraction possible [34]. Regressing the squared relative deviation of an apparent growth statistic on inverse case count across units, and reading the intercept as transmission variance or an error floor and the slope as counting noise, applies the classical decomposition to such data. Whether those readings hold has to be checked against data with a known truth, and Section 4 reports that check. Section 6 discusses real-time use, reporting that depends on transmission and the choice of generation interval. Proofs, extensions and supplementary analyses, including a cross-regime check on COVID-19 counts from mainland China, are in the appendices.

2 Model and inferential targets

2.1 A branching experiment with a known observation scale

Consider one generation of transmission with n≥1 primary infections. Conditional on the reproduction number Rt>0, the offspring counts of primary cases are independent negative binomial variables [24]:

(1)

where k>0 controls individual heterogeneity. Each secondary infection is independently reported with probability ρ∈(0,1]. Summation over primary cases and binomial thinning give the law of the reported count:

(2)

Define m=ρn and Rˆt=Ct/m. The scale m is the expected reported count at Rt=1, not the realised count Ct.

The baseline assumptions are fixed, known ρ with independent reporting (H1); conditionally independent offspring as in Eq. (1) (H2); fixed, known k (H3); and a fixed or exogenous n that does not depend on transmission (H4). Write E(Rt)=R¯>0 and Var(Rt)=vR<∞. Across periods, counts are independent given the whole transmission trajectory, each with conditional law (2). These are repeated branching experiments; they do not assert that naturally evolving incidence is exogenous. Dividing by an assumed ρ0≠ρ gives conditional mean (ρ/ρ0)Rt, a multiplicative bias that more cases do not remove.

The conditional counting variance combines offspring randomness and omission. Conditioning on the total number of secondary infections splits it into (Rt+Rt2/k)/n and (1−ρ)Rt/(ρn). The term linear in Rt is therefore not purely reporting noise; it remains under complete reporting.

3 Reporting volatility and identification

3.1 Period-level reporting variation

Replace H1 by a common period-specific reporting probability pt∈[0,1], independent of Rt and of n, with known mean ρ>0 and Var(pt)=ρ2τ2 (H5). Reporting remains independent across infections given pt. Because pt lies in [0,1] with mean ρ, Var(pt)≤ρ(1−ρ) [35], so τ2≤(1−ρ)/ρ. The estimator still divides by m=ρn and does not observe pt.

Proposition 2 (Reporting volatility and second-moment nonidentification).

Under H2–H5, put Q=R¯2+vR. The first two moments of Rˆt are:

(10)

For known m, ρ and k, the single-period mean and variance in Eq. (10) depend on vR and τ2 only through U=(1+τ2)(R¯2+vR).

Given Rt and pt the estimator has mean (pt/ρ)Rt, so a shared reporting shock is not averaged away by more infections in the same period. The statement is deliberately narrow. It concerns the first two moments of one period’s count within the specified family. It does not exclude identification from full count distributions, from temporal structure under further assumptions, or from external measurements of reporting; it also assumes that reporting is independent of transmission, an assumption Section 6 relaxes.

Corollary 2 (Current and realised-mean risks with volatile reporting).

Under H2–H5, the current-value risk is:

(11)

If, in addition, the pt are independent and identically distributed, independent of the transmission trajectory, and counts are independent given both trajectories, the two mean targets have risks:

(12)

At fixed T, unobserved reporting volatility leaves the floor vH/T on the realised-mean target as m grows, so a target free of transmission variation is not free of reporting error. The crossover scale with volatile reporting, m×,H=AH/(vR+vH), is never larger than m× (Eq. (A.5)); the lower crossover accompanies a larger risk, not better surveillance. Proofs are in Appendix A.4.

3.2 From the branching experiment to surveillance counts

If the scale m is random and associated with transmission, conditional unbiasedness given (Rt,m) still yields the conditional risk:

(13)

and the conditional moments in Eq. (13) can change with scale. A constant intercept plus a constant coefficient on inverse count therefore does not follow when the count scale is itself an epidemic outcome, as it is in surveillance. Delays, aggregation, ratio denominators and changing conditional means further separate an apparent statistic from the experiment above. The rest of the paper accordingly treats empirical dispersion diagnostics as descriptive quantities and asks, with a known-truth audit, what they recover.

4 What cross-sectional dispersion diagnostics measure

4.1 Data and apparent statistics

We used the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) weekly hospital respiratory-data snapshot retrieved on 20 October 2026 and restricted influenza admissions to the 50 US states and the District of Columbia [36, 37]. Hospital participation varied during the series, including a voluntary-reporting interval from May to October 2024 before reporting became mandatory again [38]. The analysis describes this surveillance system and does not estimate an effect of the policy change.

The windows were the early-growth phases of four seasons: 1 October–26 November 2022, 7 October–23 December 2023, 9 November–28 December 2024 and 4 October–27 December 2025. Each is the contiguous national segment with weekly growth of at least 1.05 before the first turning point after the season’s admissible start; the 2024 start follows the return to mandatory reporting. The rule is a fixed definition applied identically to every season, and it was not varied in the primary analysis. Inference conditions on the selected windows, and Table 10 refits the model with growth thresholds of 1.02 and 1.10. Missing or suppressed counts were kept missing rather than set to zero. A row requires four observed counts on consecutive weekly dates, from two weeks before its denominator week through the following week.

With Ct the admissions in week t, we used two apparent statistics. The first is the weighted growth ratio:

(14)

The second is the growth-to-reproduction transform:

(15)

The transform follows the renewal relation between growth rate and reproduction number for a gamma-distributed interval [39]. Neither statistic is a true reproduction number or a posterior estimate from a renewal model [3, 10]. Rows require Dt≥5 and, for RA, Ct≥5, which leaves 1,748 state-weeks for RA and 1,756 for G.

The primary interval has mean gμ=3.6 days and standard deviation gσ=1.6 days, the household serial-interval estimate of Cowling et al. [40]. It was kept as the primary choice because it is directly estimated from influenza household transmission and is widely used in renewal-based influenza work, even though a serial interval is not a generation interval [41]. Two sensitivities use a mean of 3.2 days, either with the same coefficient of variation or with standard deviation 2.1 days; the latter is the intrinsic generation-time estimate from US household data [42]. Section 5.3 shows how much the choice matters.

4.2 The diagnostic and its three summaries

For an apparent statistic X with pooled mean X¯, define the relative squared deviation and its affine working model

(16)

For G, Dt of Eq. (14) replaces Ct. This is the empirical counterpart of V(m)/R¯2 in Eq. (3), but with a realised count in place of the expected scale and an apparent statistic in place of Rˆt. Three summaries of the fit of Eq. (16) follow.

The intercept a is the count-independent relative dispersion. It measures the sum of all relative variation in the diagnostic statistic that does not scale with count. When reporting probabilities do not vary from week to week (τ=0), a estimates the relative variance of transmission, v˜R=vR/R¯2. When reporting shocks vary between weeks, a estimates v˜R+v˜H, where v˜H is the relative variance that the shocks induce in the ratio statistic; a reporting level that is constant over consecutive weeks cancels in the ratio (Appendix A.6). By Proposition 2, single-period cross-sectional moments cannot separate the two components. The intercept is therefore not an estimate of an error floor. With τ=0 the current-value error floor is zero, and with τ>0 the floor v˜H does not exceed a, which is only an upper bound for it. Below we call a the count-independent relative dispersion, or the relative dispersion for short.

The counting slope b is read against two references. A delta expansion of Eq. (15) under independent Poisson counts in consecutive weeks gives the independent-Poisson reference bP=κ(g)2[1+(Ct+0.5)/(Ct+1+0.5)]¯, a weighted mean over rows, with κ(g)=(gμ/7)/[1+θlog(g)/7] and g=(Ct+1+0.5)/(Ct+0.5). For the primary sample bP=0.4455. The term 1 is the Poisson variance of the denominator count. In a branching chain the denominator week contains the parents of the numerator week, so conditioning on the realised parents removes the transmission part of that variance and leaves only the binomial reporting part, (1−ρ)/Ct. With Poisson offspring and reporting probability ρ this gives the branching-Poisson reference and its ratio to bP:

(17)

The row-level ratio r(ρ) falls to 1/(1+g)≈0.42 at ρ=1 for the geometric-mean growth g0=1.407. Averaged over the observed rows, r(ρ) is 0.944, 0.861, 0.722 and 0.443 for ρ=0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 (Table S4). The two references correspond to the two estimators of Section 2. The observed-denominator model of Section 2.3, whose denominator noise (1−ρ)/m is the reporting part only, has the structure of the branching-Poisson reference, and the known-scale estimator of Section 2.1 is its limit without denominator noise. The independent-Poisson reference is the limit ρ→0, in which the denominator is an independent Poisson count. The ratio b/bP therefore asks whether counting variation exceeds independent-Poisson noise, and b/bP,br(ρ) asks the same question for a branching chain, at a reporting probability that the data do not identify.

The third summary is the dispersion-to-counting crossover count b/a, the count at which the fitted counting term equals the relative dispersion and the empirical analogue of m×. It is defined on the apparent statistic’s count scale, in admissions per week, and differs from m×, which refers to the expected count of a branching experiment.

The affine mean was fitted by iterated feasible generalised least squares with weights inversely proportional to the squared fitted mean, which minimises a gamma quasi-deviance; this is an estimating criterion, not a distributional claim. Intervals are percentiles of state-by-week pigeonhole bootstrap draws in which each row receives the product of independently drawn state and week multiplicities [43], a resampling counterpart of two-way cluster-robust inference [44]; the pooled mean and the regression are re-estimated in every draw. The primary bootstrap has 2,000 draws, and every pooled row in every table uses its weights. The within-state and two-way slopes, the season models, the generation-interval sensitivity and the sensitivity specifications also use 2,000 draws. The two- and three-week block versions of the fixed-effects decomposition, which check sensitivity to persistent national shocks, use 1,000 draws each, as do the thinning analysis of the data and the held-out validation. Draws whose iterated fit does not converge are dropped, and their number is reported with each table.

The audit below shows that these bootstrap intervals are conservative, so a second interval was calibrated for the headline summaries. It is the two-way cluster-robust sandwich of Cameron et al. [44] for the stacked estimating equations of the pooled mean and the affine fit, clustered by state and by calendar week. Small-sample factors G/(G−1) are applied, critical values come from the t distribution on 41 degrees of freedom, one fewer than the 42 weeks, and the interval for b/a is formed on the log scale. A variance-ratio-scaled bootstrap, in which the percentile interval is shrunk towards the point estimate by the bootstrap-to-Monte-Carlo standard deviation ratio of the other coverage generators, was the alternative. The rule for choosing between them was fixed before the coverage runs: the sandwich is used if its coverage of the estimator mean is at least 0.925 under every coverage generator, and the scaled bootstrap otherwise. The same sandwich gives the covariance of the season intercepts, and the season test is referred to a simulated null distribution (Section 4.4).

Binomial thinning provides a fourth check. Each unique state-week count is thinned once to Bin(C,q) for q∈{0.8,0.6,0.5,0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1}, and the thinned value is reused in every ratio that contains it. Recomputing the statistic and the fit, with the original Ct as regressor, gives the thinning response:

(18)

Under the delta approximation c=bP whatever the original counting variation, because thinning adds known binomial variance. The ratio c/bP is therefore a check of that approximation and not of the data-generating process (Appendix B.4).

4.3 Known-truth audit on the real design

The audit is a simulation study with known truth and is reported under the aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures structure of Morris et al. [45]. Its aim is to establish what a, b, b/a and c recover on the sampling design of the application. Synthetic counts were generated on the exact RA design: the 1,748 rows, 1,969 unique state-weeks and 210 state runs of the data. Each run is simulated as a whole with shared counts, so that one week’s count is the next week’s denominator. The expected count is carried forward by the true growth factors, and the geometric-mean observed growth g0=1.407 is used for transitions that are not scored. The simulated Ct serves as the count scale, the filter Ct≥5 is re-applied, and the estimand of each row is the transform (15) of its true growth factor.

Two alignment steps fix the level of the synthetic panels, and the quantities they fix are calibration targets rather than tests. Each run is level-anchored to the geometric mean of its observed counts, and one scale factor per generator, between 0.797 and 0.844, sets the Monte Carlo mean of the median retained count to the observed median of 45. In every generator with transmission heterogeneity, the amplitude of that heterogeneity is then set so that the Monte Carlo mean of the fitted intercept equals the observed a. The slope ratio b/bP, the crossover b/a, the thinning rate, the ratio of pooled to within-state slope, the reduction of a under week centring and the score contrast between affine and power-law fits are not targeted and serve as tests. A generator passes a test when the observed point value lies inside its 2.5–97.5% Monte Carlo range, and passes the score contrast when the observed contrast lies between the 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles of its simulated contrasts. This decision rule and the week-centring test were fixed after the generators had first been compared with the data, and Table 7 applies them to every generator. The lower tail of the retained counts matches the data (10th percentiles 10–11 against 10). The upper tail does not, since the generators’ 90th percentiles are 263–324 against 389 observed (Table 5). Post-stratifying retained rows to the observed deciles of the count changes intercept recovery from 1.007 to 1.008 under S1, from 1.115 to 1.079 under S4, from 1.009 to 1.004 under S6 and from 0.684 to 0.665 under S7a, so the truncated tail moves recovery by at most 3.2%. Because the implied transmission relative standard deviation scales with the inverse square root of the recovery ratio, the reweighting moves it by at most 1.7%, far less than the width of the ranges reported below.

Table 4 sets out the design. The eleven generators span the mechanisms that the diagnostics are meant to separate, from independent Poisson counts (S0) to scale-dependent heterogeneity combined with state-week reporting shocks (S8). A twelfth generator, S9, is S8 with half of the transmission heterogeneity carried by the national calendar-week component of S4 and S5. It was added after the first eleven had been compared with the data, and neither its share nor its week factor was tuned to them.

S6S3 with a state-week reporting shock ρst=0.25zst, logzst∼N(−s2/2,s2), s=0.122
S7a, S7bS3 with heterogeneity σ2(μ)=σ02(μ/45)−γ for expected count μ, γ=0.25 and 0.5
S8S3 with scale-dependent heterogeneity (γ=0.25) and state-week reporting shocks (s=0.133)
S9S8 with half of the transmission heterogeneity carried by the national-week component of S4 (s=0.132)

In S6, S8 and S9 the shock scale is chosen so that transmission and the shock each carry about half of the variance target set by the observed a, the ϕ=0.5 cell of the share grid. Tests are statistics that no alignment step targets.

Each generator was run on 200 panels, so the quantile of an observed value among simulated values has a resolution of 0.005; the score-contrast quantiles pool five independent streams of 200 panels and are reported with binomial Monte Carlo standard errors. Thinning used 100 panels with 20 draws per level. Every panel passes through the same filters and fitting functions as the data. The audit covers RA; the G statistic was not audited.

Two further designs address the questions that the generator list leaves open. A grid over the share ϕ of the total relative variance carried by transmission, ϕ∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}, crossed with scale dependence γ∈{0,0.25,0.5}, uses 1,000 panels per cell, with the remainder 1−ϕ carried by state-week reporting shocks. In its calibrated rows the amplitude makes the mean intercept equal the observed one; an uncalibrated block at γ=0.25 fixes the total variance at the observed a and tests a as well. A coverage study analyses 400 panels from each of S1, S6, S8 and S9 exactly as the data, with 200 pigeonhole bootstrap draws per panel, and records whether each nominal 95% interval covers its target. The same 400 panels per generator calibrate the two-way sandwich and the season test; under the season null each season intercept is centred at its Monte Carlo mean.

Two designs complete the tests. A second share grid crosses ϕ and γ with a national calendar-week share of the transmission draw of 0 or 0.5, giving 30 cells, and applies all six tests to each cell with the decision rule of the audit. In each cell with heterogeneity the amplitude is also recalibrated to the lower and upper limits of the calibrated interval for a, so that the transmission relative standard deviation implied by the observed intercept carries the uncertainty in a. A held-out reference repeats the leave-one-state-out and leave-one-season-out score comparison of Section 5.4 on 200 synthetic panels from every generator, with the folds, rows and score of the data.

The estimand of the audit is operational. The intercept a is compared with the relative variance of the transmission factor on the retained rows of each simulated panel, v˜R, and, when reporting shocks are present, with the total v˜R+v˜H. These are finite-population quantities of the panel, not parameters of a superpopulation of states or seasons [27]. Interval coverage is judged against the Monte Carlo mean of each estimator, which a dependence-aware resampling scheme can target, and separately against the true total. The targets of Section 2 map onto these quantities only under the conditions of Section 3. With reporting fixed, v˜R is the between-row variation that a current-value analysis resolves; with volatile reporting the total bounds the error floor of the current value.

4.4 Audit results

Without reporting shocks the intercept tracks the relative variance of transmission. When transmission is constant (S0, S2 and S2P) the fitted intercept is essentially zero, so b/a is undefined. With independent heterogeneity, the ratio of a to the true relative variance of Ri on the retained rows is 1.01 (Monte Carlo range 0.93–1.09) under S1 and 1.02 (0.91–1.13) under S3. With structured heterogeneity it is 1.12 (1.04–1.19) under S4 and 1.15 (1.06–1.27) under S5 (Table 5; Fig. 2C), because crossed state and national-week components partially project onto the marginal intercept. Fitting the same affine model to the true estimation error, ((X−Ri)/X¯)2, gives an intercept of about 3×10−5 in each of these generators, so the current-value error floor is essentially zero without reporting shocks. Week centring removes 62% of a under S4 and 59% under S5, where half of the heterogeneity is national, and essentially none under S1 and S3.

With reporting shocks the intercept is the sum of both components. Under S6, a is 1.01 (0.87–1.14) times the total v˜R+v˜H and 2.02 (1.71–2.29) times v˜R alone. The true-error intercept is 1.02 (0.83–1.19) times v˜H, so the current-value error floor equals the shock component and is about half of a. The shock terms of consecutive rows have correlation −0.50 (−0.53 to −0.46), because a shock in one week enters the numerator of one row and the denominator of the next. Scale-dependent heterogeneity biases the intercept in the other direction. Under S7a and S7b it is 0.68 (0.60–0.78) and 0.43 (0.37–0.50) times the true relative variance, because variation that shrinks with count is absorbed by the slope. Under S8 the two distortions combine, and a is 1.75 (1.47–2.04) times v˜R and 0.85 (0.72–0.99) times the total.

The counting slope does not identify the mechanism. The ratio b/bP is 0.93 (0.85–1.01) under S0, 0.80 (0.73–0.86) under S2P and 1.23 (1.13–1.32) under S2 (Table 6; Fig. 2A). The gamma quasi-likelihood slope therefore falls about 7% short of the analytic reference under independent Poisson counts, and the simulated-to-analytic ratio is 0.91–0.93 for every reference in Table S4. The step from S0 to S2P reflects the structure of denominator noise. In a branching chain only the reporting part of the denominator noise remains, as the branching-Poisson reference predicts (r(0.25)=0.861, simulated 0.802). The step from S2P to S2 is offspring overdispersion. Transmission heterogeneity moves the ratio in both directions. It is 0.85 (0.69–1.02) under S1, 1.14 (0.98–1.31) under S3, 0.73 (0.60–0.87) under S4, 1.03 (0.87–1.20) under S5 and 1.14 (0.97–1.34) under S6. Scale-dependent heterogeneity raises it to 1.56 (1.34–1.79) under S7a, 2.25 (1.98–2.58) under S7b and 1.31 (1.08–1.52) under S8. A slope near or above bP is therefore compatible with several combinations of overdispersion, reporting and heterogeneity. Structured heterogeneity also lowers the within-state slope below the pooled slope, although counting noise is the same in every state. Under S4 the ratio of pooled to within-state slope is 1.14 (0.99–1.37), and in the other generators it lies between 1.01 and 1.10. The observed point ratio, 1.48, lies outside the Monte Carlo range of every generator, although its interval, 0.99–3.66, reaches 1.

The crossover count does not discriminate between mechanisms either. Among generators with heterogeneity, b/a ranges from 22.2 (17.0–27.7) under S4 to 42.1 (30.8–58.2) under S8, against 51.4 (39.5–65.9) and 77.5 (58.4–99.7) under S7a and S7b. The observed value, 37.4, lies within the S3, S5, S6 and S8 ranges, and both its bootstrap interval, 18.4–72.4, and its calibrated two-way interval, 24.1–58.3, overlap all eight.

The curve shape separates generators more sharply than either slope summary. The in-sample difference in quasi-deviance score between affine and power-law fits is close to zero under S0, S2 and S2P, whose intercept is zero. Generators with heterogeneity that does not depend on count give differences from 0.012 (S1) to 0.024 (S5) in favour of the affine form, whereas the observed difference is −0.0014. At most 0.3% of their panels reach a contrast this low (Fig. 2D). Under S7a the observed contrast lies at the 0.495 quantile, but the S7a slope ratio range (1.34–1.79) excludes the observed 1.257. Under S8 the observed contrast lies at the 0.069 quantile (Monte Carlo standard error 0.008), and the observed crossover and slope ratio lie inside the S8 ranges. S8 does not reproduce the two remaining tests. Its pooled-to-within slope ratio ranges from 0.92 to 1.15 against the observed 1.48, and week centring changes its a by −6.1% to 2.3% against the observed reduction of 34.7%. S9, which adds a national calendar-week component to S8, raises the week-centring reduction to 19.1% (12.5–25.9), still below the observed value, and leaves the slope-ratio range at 0.92–1.17; its observed contrast quantile is 0.057 (0.007). No generator passes every test, and S8 and S9 pass four of six (Table 7). The contrast comparison is in sample, but its held-out version points the same way (Table S18). Leaving one state out, the observed power-minus-affine contrast, −0.0020, lies below every simulated panel under S1, S3, S4, S5 and S6, whose mean held-out contrasts are 0.011–0.024 in favour of the affine form, at the 0.125–0.475 quantiles of S0, S2, S2P and S7a, and at the 0.995 quantile of S7b. Under S8 and S9 it lies at the 0.050 (0.015) and 0.055 (0.016) quantiles, inside the decision rule but in the lower tail. With only four folds, the leave-one-season-out contrast discriminates weakly: its observed value, 0.0046, lies inside the central 95% of S0, S1, S6, S7a, S8 and S9 and outside it for the other six generators. The near-zero held-out state contrast, which on its own does not separate the two forms, is therefore unlikely under heterogeneity that does not depend on count. The simulated panels also retain 1,596 (S8) and 1,571 (S9) rows on average against 1,748 observed, and their upper count tail is shorter than the observed one. The audited generators therefore bracket the data on most summaries without reproducing all of them, and the data, which do not trace infections longitudinally, cannot identify the data-generating process.

The share grid shows how much the compatible region leaves open (Table S1; Fig. 3). Among calibrated cells, the observed slope ratio, crossover and contrast all fall inside the simulated ranges only at γ=0.25 with ϕ=0.25, 0.5 and 0.75, and at γ=0.5 with ϕ=0.5. Across these cells the intercept is 1.04–3.85 times the transmission relative variance and 0.74–0.94 times the total. Two of the compatible cells are borderline on the contrast, with quantiles of 0.026 and 0.024 (standard error 0.005). Without scale dependence (γ=0) every share is excluded by the contrast, and with scale dependence pure transmission (ϕ=1) is excluded by the slope ratio and the crossover. Within the compatible region the transmission share is not identified. In the uncalibrated block, where the total variance is fixed at the observed a, only the cells with ϕ≤0.25 keep a inside its range, and the contrast excludes both.

Under all six tests no cell of the extended grid reproduces the data (Table S2). The pooled/within slope ratio fails in all 30 cells: the largest simulated upper limit is 1.25 against the observed 1.48. Week centring passes in three cells, all with a national share of 0.5, and the contrast in 12. The best cell, γ=0.25, ϕ=0.75 with a national share of 0.5, passes five of the six tests, and its implied transmission relative standard deviation is 11.5% (9.9–13.0% when the uncertainty in a is propagated). Nine cells pass the slope ratio, the crossover and the contrast, the tests of the first grid; thinning excludes none of them. Their implied relative standard deviation is 6.2–13.9% at the observed a and 5.3–15.5% with the uncertainty in a propagated, against 5.1–20.5% across all 25 cells with heterogeneity. Of the 180 pass or fail decisions, 19 lie within two Monte Carlo standard errors of a limit. The range remains conditional on k=0.3 and ρ=0.25 and on a family that does not reproduce the pooled-to-within slope ratio.

The bootstrap intervals are conservative for their estimands (Table 8). Across S1, S6, S8 and S9, intervals for a, b and b/a cover the Monte Carlo mean of the corresponding estimator in at least 99.5% of panels, against a nominal 95%. The mean bootstrap standard deviation is 1.6–2.5 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation of the point estimates, in line with the conservative variance of the pigeonhole bootstrap under crossed designs [43]. Coverage of the true total relative variance by the interval for a is 1.000 under S1 and 0.998 under S6, but falls to 0.892 (0.015) under S8. That shortfall comes from the estimator and not from the interval, because the mean of a under S8 is 0.857 times the total. Under S9, which adds crossed state and national-week dependence, the intervals cover the estimator means in 0.998 (a), 1.000 (b) and 0.998 (b/a) of panels and the true total in 0.963 (0.009), with the mean of a at 0.889 times the total. The bootstrap intervals are therefore wide rather than calibrated.

The two-way sandwich meets the decision rule, and it is the calibrated interval reported for a, b and b/a (Table 9). Its coverage of the estimator mean for a is 0.993 (0.004) under S1, 0.925 (0.013) under S6 and S8, and 0.983 (0.007) under S9; for b it is 0.917–0.945 and for b/a 0.915–0.970. The rule was applied to a; because the coverage for b and b/a falls slightly below 0.925 under S6, the bootstrap intervals are reported alongside the sandwich intervals for all three summaries. Under S6 and S8 the coverage of a equals the threshold, so the rule is met without margin. The mean sandwich standard error of a is 0.94–1.40 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation. Because the sandwich interval is centred on a biased estimator under S8, it covers the true total in only 0.42 of S8 panels, against 0.93 under S6. The scaled bootstrap covers the estimator mean for a in 0.915–0.990 of panels and would have failed the rule under S8.

The season test needs the same calibration. Its Wald statistic with the sandwich covariance is liberal at the χ32 critical value, rejecting a true null in 0.195 (0.020) of S6 panels and 0.217 (0.021) of S8 panels, and the simulated 95th percentile of the null statistic is 6.8–16.5 across generators against 7.8 for χ32. With the bootstrap covariance the statistic is very conservative, with a simulated null 95th percentile of 1.3–2.7 and no rejection at the χ32 critical value. The observed season statistics are referred to these simulated null distributions in Section 5.3. The generators carry less dependent variation than the data, however. The observed two-way standard error of a is 1.7–2.9 times the Monte Carlo standard deviation of a under the four generators, and the observed relative standard errors of the season intercepts, 0.17–0.25, exceed the generators’ Monte Carlo standard deviations of logas, 0.07–0.15. The calibration therefore transfers to the data only if the null distribution of the statistic is insensitive to that scale.

5 Application to US influenza hospital admissions

5.1 Count-independent relative dispersion

For RA the pooled affine fit gave a=0.0150 (calibrated two-way 95% confidence interval 0.0109–0.0191) and b=0.560 (0.430–0.690); the conservative bootstrap intervals are 0.0101–0.0206 and 0.362–0.769 (primary row of Table 10; Table 9). The count-independent relative dispersion a corresponds to a relative SD of about 12% around the pooled mean of RA. It is not by itself an estimate of transmission variance, because the audit shows that the intercept recovers different quantities under different mechanisms (Section 4.4). Read through the recovery ratio of each audited generator with heterogeneity, the observed intercept implies a transmission relative SD from 9% (S6) to 19% (S7b). Under reporting shocks of the S8 and S9 kinds the intercept overstates transmission variance by a factor of 1.75–1.84 and implies 9%, whereas under scale-dependent heterogeneity (S7a, S7b) it understates it. In the share grid no cell passes all six tests. Restricted to the cells that pass the slope ratio, the crossover and the contrast, the implied transmission relative SD is 6–14% at the observed a and 5–16% when the uncertainty in a is propagated, and the share of a carried by transmission is not identified (Tables S1 and S2). These figures are conditional on the audited mechanisms, none of which passes every test (Table 7). The renewal growth statistic G is reported in Appendix Table S3 as an un-audited descriptive comparison on the weighted denominator Dt.

Week centring, which replaces the pooled mean by the national mean of each calendar week, reduced a by 34.7% (6.0–51.9) for RA and by 33.3% (6.8–51.6) for G (Table S8; Fig. S2). Leaving the own state out of the weekly centre gave nearly the same values. Season means and season-specific linear trends left a almost unchanged. In the audit, week centring removed almost nothing when transmission heterogeneity was independent across states (−2.8% to 0.4% in S1, S3, S6, S7a and S7b) and removed 61.8% (S4) and 58.6% (S5) when half of it was national. The observed reduction lies between these values, which is consistent with a partly synchronous national component of intermediate size. Under S9, in which half of the transmission heterogeneity is national and reporting shocks carry half of the variance target, the reduction is 19.1% (12.5–25.9), below the observed value. Adjusting for hospital reporting participation changed a by 0.00029 (−0.00032 to 0.00085) (Table S9). Off-season summer weeks, outside the analysis windows, are described in Table S14. Reporting was voluntary only in summer 2024, when median participation was 45.6% against 92.3–94.2% in the other two summers. The interquartile range of logG was then 0.67 against 0.49, a descriptive contrast.

5.2 Counting slope

The pooled counting slope was 1.26 (0.81–1.73) times the independent-Poisson reference, 26% above it with an interval that includes 1. Against the branching-Poisson reference of Eq. (17) the ratio was 1.46 (0.94–2.02) at ρ=0.25 and 2.84 (1.83–3.94) at ρ=1 relative to the analytic reference; relative to the simulated reference, which shares the finite-sample bias of the fitting procedure, the ratios are about 1.57 and 3.13 (Table S4). The excess over a branching-Poisson reference therefore depends on the reporting probability, which the slope itself does not identify.

Within-unit estimates were lower and less precise (Table S10; Fig. 5B). A state fixed-effects fit gave 0.85 (0.24–1.47) bP by iterated weighting and 1.02 (0.51–1.53) by a one-step weighted fit; a damped iterated two-way fit gave 0.93 (0.09–1.48) bP, with 1,962 of 2,000 bootstrap draws converging, and its one-step counterpart 1.08 (0.47–1.66). The undamped two-way iteration oscillated between two values and did not converge. A week fixed-effects fit gave 1.42 (0.96–1.89) bP.

The pooled and state fixed-effects fits can also be compared through their crossover counts. The cross-count ratio, pooled b/a divided by state fixed-effects b over mean state intercept, was 2.16 (0.99–7.64). It factorises exactly into a slope ratio, pooled b over state fixed-effects b, of 1.48 (0.99–3.66), and an intercept ratio, mean state intercept over pooled a, of 1.47 (0.99–2.29); the slope ratio accounts for half of the log cross-count ratio (0.50, 0.31–0.74) (Table S11). Under single-week resampling all three intervals include 1; under two-week blocks all three still do, and under three-week blocks the three lower limits are 1.01–1.03. In the audit, generator S4, in which all states share one counting process, gave a pooled-to-within slope ratio of 1.14 (Monte Carlo range 0.99–1.37) (Table 6). Structured heterogeneity alone thus raises the pooled slope above the within-state slope. The observed slope ratio lies above the S4 value, but its interval overlaps the S4 range, so between-state differences in counting remain unresolved.

The counting slope also does not identify reporting probability or offspring dispersion. With independent transmission heterogeneity of the S1 kind, the expected b/bP ranged from 0.37 (Poisson offspring, ρ=1) to 2.89 (k=0.1, ρ=1) across four reporting probabilities and five offspring laws (Fig. 4; Table S12). The observed interval contains the expected value in 10 of the 20 cells, namely all five offspring laws at ρ=0.1, k=1 at every reporting probability and k=0.3 at ρ=0.25 and 0.5. Very different combinations of under-reporting and superspreading are compatible with the same slope, and heterogeneity of the S4 kind would lower the expected slopes (S4 0.73 against S1 0.85 in Table 6).

5.3 Dispersion-to-counting crossover count

The dispersion-to-counting crossover count was b/a=37.4 admissions per week for RA, with a calibrated two-way interval of 24.1–58.3 and a bootstrap interval of 18.4–72.4; the sensitivity intervals below are bootstrap intervals. The point estimate was 49.7 (25.0–96.6) when rows required Ct≥10 (1,535 rows), 52.8 (19.0–122.9) at Ct≥20 (1,203 rows) and 53.1 (−8.4 to 180.1) at Ct≥50 (776 rows), where the ratio was nonpositive in 4.8% of draws. A continuity correction of 1.0 instead of 0.5 gave 33.1 (16.3–66.3) and a window threshold of 1.10 gave 38.6 (20.6–70.3) on 1,564 rows (Table 10; Fig. 5A). The value 37.4 is an in-sample descriptive crossover for this panel and window rule, not a sample-size rule for surveillance.

Each row refits the affine FGLS on the subset or variant with a state-week bootstrap; the primary row is the primary bootstrap (2,000 draws, identical to Table S3), the other rows use 2,000 draws each. Where b/a ≤ 0 (b ≤ 0) in more than 2.5% of draws its percentile interval is unstable; draws whose FGLS fit did not converge are dropped and counted. The growth-window rule 1.02 selects the same 1,748 rows as the primary rule, so its row differs from the primary row only through the bootstrap draws.

Fitted separately, the four seasons gave 50.9, 113.7, 45.9 and 15.7 on 365, 499, 356 and 528 rows. These values are descriptive, and each has a wide interval, from 4.1–71.6 in 2025–26 to 30.2–315.1 in 2023–24. A model with season-specific intercepts and a common slope (b=0.607, 0.415–0.794) gave season crossover counts of 38.3, 85.7, 39.5 and 33.7 (Table S13). With a common slope, equal season intercepts are equivalent to equal season crossover counts. The test of equality is a Wald test on log intercepts, chosen because the intercepts are strictly positive and multiplicative differences are the quantity of interest. Referred to χ32, the statistic with the inter-season bootstrap covariance gave W=5.52 (p=0.138). Cochran’s Q, evaluated using diagonal inverse-variance weights without off-diagonal covariance, was 4.57 (p=0.206, I2=34%). On the raw intercept scale the Wald test gave p=0.064, and a test on separate season fits gave p=0.220. These χ2 references are not calibrated, because the bootstrap covariance is conservative (Section 4.4). Referred to the simulated null distributions of the four coverage generators, W=5.52 exceeds every simulated null statistic (calibrated p<0.005), and the statistic with the two-way sandwich covariance, WCGM=17.8, has calibrated p values of 0.005–0.045 (Table 9). Under each of these calibrations the test rejects equal season intercepts at the 5% level. The difference comes mainly from the second season (2023–24), whose fitted intercept was 0.0071 against 0.0154–0.0180 in the others, which pushes its crossover count to 85.7. The rejection is conditional on the calibration. The generators carry less dependent variation than the data (Section 4.4), so the calibrated p values may be too small. Under the uncalibrated χ32 reference with the bootstrap covariance the test has limited power: reaching 80% power at the 5% level along the observed pattern requires the deviations to be 1.41 times larger, corresponding to a pattern-specific minimum detectable ratio of 3.71 between the highest and lowest season intercepts, against the observed 2.54. Even when differences are detected, the between-season variance itself can be estimated only to a relative SE of at least 0.82 with four seasons (Appendix B.3).

The interval choice has almost no effect on the ratio. Replacing the primary interval with a mean of 3.2 days changed b/a by 0.17 (−0.65 to 0.89), and the intrinsic generation-time estimate with standard deviation 2.1 days changed it by 0.49 (−2.55 to 3.04), with b/bP 1.27 and 1.23 (Table S15). The interval rescales a and b together, so it affects the levels of the two summaries but not their ratio.

5.4 Shape of the dispersion curve

Held-out comparison of the affine model with a power law λC−γ did not separate the two forms. Leaving out one state at a time, the power-minus-affine score difference was −0.0020 (paired standard error 0.0068), with 26 of 51 folds favouring the affine model. Leaving out one season at a time it was 0.0046 (0.0087), with 3 of 4 folds favouring the affine model (Tables S17 and S19; Fig. S3). The held-out state contrast nevertheless discriminates between mechanisms. On synthetic panels analysed with the same folds, generators with heterogeneity that does not depend on count favour the affine form by 0.011–0.024 on average, and none of their panels reaches a contrast as low as the observed one. The observed value is typical of the generators without heterogeneity and of S7a, and lies at the 0.050 and 0.055 quantiles of S8 and S9 (Table S18). Out of sample, as in sample, the data therefore weigh against count-independent heterogeneity without favouring either form as a law. The affine form is used here as a working summary, not as an established law for surveillance dispersion.

6 Discussion

The theoretical part of the paper makes one distinction precise. With fixed, known reporting, exogenous exposure and conditionally independent counting errors, the risk for the current value is A/m and the risk for the realised mean of the observed periods is A/(Tm). The process mean adds the variance of the realised mean, which more cases within the same periods do not reduce. The count at which counting error equals between-period variance is the half-weight point of the corresponding shrinkage estimator, as in small-area estimation and disease mapping [14, 15]. It belongs with its estimator, target and sampling experiment and is not a property of a pathogen. The efficiency statement holds within a class of conditionally unbiased estimators with a known denominator. Information from other features of the epidemic curve [6, 46], independent reporting measurements or prior structure changes what can be learned, and estimators that accept bias in exchange for lower variance lie outside that class. Appendix B gives the corresponding forecast weight, the allocation of a fixed budget between periods and cases, and a lower bound on the precision with which a few seasons can estimate between-season variation.

The empirical part shows what can and cannot be read from a cross-sectional dispersion curve. Its intercept is a count-independent relative dispersion, the part of the variation in the statistic that does not scale with the count. With reporting fixed across weeks it is the relative variance of transmission across units and weeks; with week-to-week reporting shocks it also contains their contribution, and single-period moments cannot split the two (Proposition 2). For influenza admissions it is about 0.015, which implies a transmission relative standard deviation between 6% and 19% across the audited generators and share-grid cells, and between 5% and 20% across the grid once the uncertainty in the intercept is propagated. The range is conditional on those mechanisms, none of which reproduces every tested summary. Under fixed reporting this is the variation that a current-value analysis wants to resolve and that a process-mean analysis treats as sampling variation; under volatile reporting it is an upper bound on the error floor of the current value. The counting slope, its ratio to the independent-Poisson or branching-Poisson reference and the thinning response cannot distinguish overdispersed offspring, under-reporting and heterogeneous transmission. The audit produces slopes near the observed one under several combinations, and the grid over ρ and k admits values from heavy under-reporting with strong superspreading to near-complete reporting with moderate dispersion. The dispersion-to-counting crossover count was about 37 admissions per week for the pooled panel. Equal season intercepts were rejected once the test was referred to a simulated null distribution, mainly because of a lower intercept in 2023–24, but that calibration rests on generators with less dependent variation than the data, and with four seasons the between-season variance itself remains poorly estimated. The crossover marks where counting noise stops dominating the cross-sectional dispersion of this statistic, not where additional cases stop being useful for a particular target.

6.1 Real-time estimation

All analyses used a retrospective snapshot in which counts are close to final. In real time, reporting delays leave the most recent weeks incomplete, and right-censoring biases the latest counts downwards in proportion to the delay distribution [47, 48]. The current-value target is affected first and most, because its risk is dominated by the last one or two periods, exactly those that are incomplete, whereas a realised or process mean over many periods dilutes them. The RA statistic also needs Ct+1, so it is available only one week after its reference week, and estimates near the end of a series combine smaller effective counts with nowcasting uncertainty. Real-time renewal methods address this by modelling delays and the infection process jointly [2, 49, 50]. In the present framework, nowcasting adds a correction-error term to the counting term, and its variance grows as the delay distribution places more mass beyond the current week. A crossover count estimated from retrospective data will therefore overstate the precision available in real time.

Estimation windows raise a related issue. Widening a window in renewal estimators accumulates incidence while imposing constancy of the reproduction number over a longer interval [2, 3]. This trades temporal resolution for precision and is not equivalent to observing more independent periods; the averages in Table 2 instead give each period its own transmission value. Applying their formulas to overlapping windows requires explicit treatment of the overlap.

6.2 Reporting that depends on transmission

Proposition 2 assumes that the reporting probability is independent of transmission. In practice testing, care seeking and admission thresholds can change with epidemic activity [51, 52]. Write zt=pt/ρ for the relative reporting probability. Given Rt, the estimator then has conditional bias

(19)

By Eq. (19), if reporting rises with transmission, so that Cov(zt,Rt)>0, high-transmission periods are over-counted and low-transmission periods under-counted, the estimated swings exaggerate the true ones, and the fitted intercept overstates the relative dispersion of transmission. If reporting falls with transmission, for example when admission capacity saturates or testing is rationed at the peak, the estimates damp the swings and the intercept understates it. In both cases the process-mean estimate is biased by Cov(zt,Rt), and the bias does not shrink with more cases. Neither direction can be detected from the counts alone; it requires external information on testing or admission practice. The participation adjustment used here addresses only facility participation, and it changed the intercept negligibly.

6.3 Choice of interval distribution

The transform in Eq. (15) needs an interval distribution. We kept the household serial interval of Cowling et al. [40] as the primary choice because it is directly estimated for influenza, widely used and fixed before the analyses reported here. The intrinsic generation-time estimate of Chan et al. [42], the more appropriate quantity for a renewal mapping, served as a sensitivity analysis. Serial intervals, intrinsic generation intervals and realised household generation intervals are different quantities [41], and the mapping from growth rate to reproduction number depends on which is used [39]. The levels of a and b change with the interval, but their ratio and the slope ratio to the independent-Poisson reference change by less than their sampling uncertainty, so the conclusions about what the diagnostics measure do not depend on this choice.

6.4 Identification and limitations

Separating the mechanisms behind the dispersion curve requires information that a single cross-section lacks. Temporal structure can separate persistent transmission variation from independent counting and reporting noise under explicit state-space or renewal models [30, 31, 53], and external measurements of reporting can constrain ρ and its variation. The shape of the curve narrows the candidates without identifying one. The observed power-minus-affine contrast lay at or below the 0.3% quantile of every generator whose heterogeneity does not depend on count (S1 and S3–S6). Scale-dependent heterogeneity alone (S7a) reproduces the contrast but not the slope ratio. Scale-dependent heterogeneity combined with reporting shocks (S8) reproduces the intercept, the crossover count, the slope ratio and the contrast, and the share grid shows a family of such combinations. Within that family the intercept is between 1.04 and 3.85 times the transmission relative variance, so the share of a due to transmission remains unidentified. The held-out state contrast gives the same ordering: it is improbable under count-independent heterogeneity and lies in the lower tail of S8 and S9. No mechanism in the audit or the grid reproduces the gap between pooled and within-state slopes, and week centring is reproduced only where part of the heterogeneity is national, so the family is an approximation and not a description of the data-generating process. Reporting that varies with jurisdiction size would leave the same trace.

The growth windows are a fixed rule applied to four seasons of one surveillance system, and inference conditions on that selection; window thresholds of 1.02 and 1.10 left the crossover count at 37.4 and 38.6, and transfer of these values to other epidemic regimes would need data from those regimes. The analyses used a retrospective snapshot, so reporting delays and right-censoring of recent weeks were not modelled (Section 6.1). The audit generators are stylised, and their count alignment matched the median and lower tail of the observed counts more closely than the upper tail, although reweighting to the observed count deciles changed the intercept recovery by at most 3.2%. The (ρ,k) grid used independent heterogeneity only, and the growth statistic G was not audited. The pigeonhole bootstrap intervals were conservative in the audit, with standard deviations 1.6–2.5 times the Monte Carlo values. The two-way sandwich intervals reported for a, b and b/a met the coverage rule, but only at its threshold under S6 and S8, and intervals for other quantities remain bootstrap intervals. The generators used to calibrate both the intervals and the season test have less dependent variation than the data, with an observed standard error of a 1.7–2.9 times their Monte Carlo standard deviation, so the calibrated season p values may be too small. Intervals for iterated fits condition on convergence, and within-unit slopes were imprecise and sensitive to the weighting scheme. Facility participation measures only one aspect of ascertainment, and the comparison with a second reporting regime in Appendix B.5 is descriptive.

6.5 Checklist for surveillance practice

Four recommendations for reporting reproduction numbers follow from these results.

  1. State the inferential target. An estimate may target the current value Rt, the realised mean R¯T over the observed periods or the process mean R¯. Precision statements of the form A/m apply to the first two under declared reporting assumptions and omit between-period variation for the third.

  2. Inflate the counting error when the denominator is an observed count. The delta factor is 1+(1−ρ)(R¯2+vR)/A, which is 1.48 under the illustrative parameters of Section 2.3. At small counts the factor is larger, 2.42 at m=10 in Table 3. The half-weight count of the shrinkage estimator moves from m× to m×+(1−ρ)(R¯2+vR)/vR, from 53.1 to 78.6 under the same parameters.

  3. Qualify single-period estimates for reporting volatility. One period’s counts cannot separate transmission changes from reporting shocks (Proposition 2), so rapid changes should be checked against testing volumes, reporting participation or temporal models before they are interpreted as transmission.

  4. Treat dispersion fits as descriptive. The intercept a, the slope b and the crossover count b/a describe the observed statistic on the selected rows. They are not a transmission-variance estimate without an assumed mechanism, and b/a is not a sample-size threshold for surveillance.

7 Conclusion

The inferential target decides what additional cases buy. More cases shrink the counting error of the current value and of the realised mean of the observed periods, but they do not remove the between-period variation that limits estimation of the process mean. When reporting fluctuates from week to week, the fluctuation leaves an error floor on the current value, and single-period second moments cannot separate it from transmission variation. A known-truth simulation study on the real surveillance design shows that the intercept of a cross-sectional dispersion curve recovers transmission variance, the transmission-plus-reporting total or less than either, depending on the mechanism. Such diagnostics therefore describe a count-independent relative dispersion and the counting noise around it. Separating under-reporting, superspreading and structured transmission requires temporal models or external data on reporting.

Data and code availability

The analyses used the dataset Weekly Hospital Respiratory Data (HRD) Metrics by Jurisdiction, National Healthcare Safety Network, published by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under the identifier ua7e-t2fy [36], in the snapshot retrieved on 20 October 2026. The COVID-19 counts for mainland China are from the Johns Hopkins CSSE repository [54]. The data-processing code and analysis-window definitions are in the public repository https://github.com/wangchi2068/reproduction-number-targets-surveillance (commit 6bbb8458a5ba3a9ba644d755320df55dbe06746b). Code, data extracts, simulation settings and result files for every reported analysis are distributed with this article; running bash code/run_all.sh from the distributed experiment directory regenerates every reported estimate, table and figure from the stored inputs. No individual-level or restricted data were used.

A Proofs

A.1 Count law and conditional information

The probability generating function of one negative binomial offspring count is [1+(Rt/k)(1−z)]−k. Conditional independence raises this function to the power n, and substituting z↦1−ρ+ρz for independent reporting gives [1+(ρRt/k)(1−z)]−nk, which proves Eq. (2); its derivatives give the stated moments.

For fixed, known (n,ρ,k) and R>0, the count likelihood has score and Fisher information

(A.1)

By Eq. (A.1), Var(Rˆ∣R)=ℐ(R)−1. The support does not depend on R, so the regular one-parameter Cramér–Rao inequality applies to estimators unbiased for every R and gives the attained bound stated in Section 2.2 [23]. The bound therefore applies to estimators unbiased for every R with ρ and k known; biased estimators and unknown nuisance parameters require a separate analysis.

A.2 Proof of Proposition 1

Let et=Rˆt−Rt. The error is conditionally centred, E(et∣Rt)=0, and its second moments are as follows:

(A.2)

Squaring Eq. (4) proves Eq. (3). Any estimator based on the same count and unbiased conditional on every Rt has expected conditional variance at least E[ℐ(Rt)−1]=A/m, and its process-mean risk adds the same vR. At fixed ρ, k and transmission law, [V(m)−V(2m)]/V(m)=1/[2(1+m/m×)] for vR>0. The comparison changes exposure n; it does not hold unchanged when the reporting probability changes. The shrinkage weight in Eq. (5) is Cov(Rt,Rˆt)/Var(Rˆt)=vR/V(m).

A.3 Proof of Corollary 1

Conditional on the path R1:T, the et are independent and centred, hence pairwise uncorrelated and orthogonal to every square-integrable function of the path. Thus the average of e1,…,eT has second moment A/(Tm), and Var(Rˆ¯T)=Var(R¯T)+A/(Tm). Under the stated stationary autocovariance, summing all covariance pairs gives T2Var(R¯T)=vRS(ϕ,T) with the first expression in Eq. (7), and the finite geometric sum yields the second [55]. Summing spatial covariance pairs in the same way gives Eq. (8), for any admissible correlation matrix.

A.4 Proof of Proposition 2 and Corollary 2

Write zt=pt/ρ and ut=Ct/m−ztRt. Conditional on (Rt,pt), ut has zero mean. Independence of pt and Rt, with Ezt=1 and Ezt2=1+τ2, gives

(A.3)

The error Rˆt−Rt=ut+(zt−1)Rt has uncorrelated terms, and the second has expected square τ2(R¯2+vR)=vH, which proves Eq. (11). Because E(Rˆt−Rt∣Rt)=0, process-mean risk adds vR. Under the additional cross-period assumptions of Corollary 2, the errors are centred and independent given the transmission path after integrating out reporting, which gives Eq. (12).

For the identification statement, set U=(1+τ2)(R¯2+vR). The two moments of the scaled count are

(A.4)

Whenever distinct admissible values of τ2 give vR=U/(1+τ2)−R¯2≥0, the moments in Eq. (A.4) coincide, and varying an exogenous m does not separate them. This proves nonidentification by these moments only; it does not assert equality of full count distributions.

For vR>0, the crossover scale with volatile reporting, m×,H=AH/(vR+vH), satisfies

(A.5)

with equality exactly when τ=0.

A.5 Observed denominator

Let Mt∼Bin(n,ρ) be independent of the offspring given n, and write Mt=m(1+ut), so that Eut=0 and Var(ut)=(1−ρ)/m. Then R˜t=Rˆt/(1+ut). To first order in ut and Rˆt−Rt, the error is approximately:

(A.6)

Given (n,Rt), ut is independent of Rˆt−Rt and centred, so the cross term vanishes and E[(R˜t−Rt)2]≈A/m+(1−ρ)E(Rt2)/m, which is Eq. (9). The Monte Carlo check in Table 3 draws Rt from a gamma law with the stated moments and would discard draws with Mt=0, none of which occurred at the scales shown. The approximation neglects the convexity of 1/(1+ut), which inflates the error when m is small; at m=10 the Monte Carlo error is 1.64 times the delta value.

A.6 Reporting shocks in the ratio statistic

Let the count of week t in a state be reported with probability ρzt, where the shocks zt are independent between weeks with logzt∼N(−s2/2,s2). To first order, the statistic in Eq. (15) satisfies logRA,t≈const+κ(g)loggt with κ(g)=(gμ/7)/[1+θlog(g)/7], because αθ=gμ. The shocks enter the observed growth factor as loggt=loggttr+ηt, with ηt=logzt+1−logzt and gttr the growth factor without shocks. Hence Var(ηt)=2s2, and the relative variance that the shocks add to the ratio statistic is

(A.7)

which does not scale with count and therefore enters the intercept a. A reporting level that is constant over consecutive weeks of a state (zt+1=zt) gives ηt=0 and cancels. Consecutive rows share one shock with opposite signs, so Cov(ηt,ηt+1)=−s2 and their correlation is −1/2. The affine fit uses squared deviations, and for jointly Gaussian terms a correlation of −1/2 becomes a correlation of +1/4 between their squares. Resampling single weeks does not preserve this serial dependence, so interval coverage was checked directly. Under S6 and S8, which contain such shocks, the intervals for a, b and b/a covered the Monte Carlo means of their estimators in at least 99.5% of 400 panels (Table 8). For the realised mean over T consecutive rows of one state the mean of the shock terms telescopes to (logzT+1−logz1)/T, so their contribution to the error of the realised mean falls as T−2 rather than T−1. With κ near 0.5 for the primary interval and s=0.122 as in generator S6, Eq. (A.7) gives a shock component of about half the observed intercept.

B Extensions

B.1 Forecasting and shrinkage

Under fixed, known reporting and the stationary covariance of Corollary 1, with the counting error at t centred given the transmission path, the best forecast of Rt+1 of the form R¯+λ(Rˆt−R¯) has

(B.1)

which follows from Cov(Rˆt,Rt+1)=ϕvR. The forecast weight in Eq. (B.1) is the shrinkage weight discounted by persistence, and its limit risk is (1−ϕ2)vR. For the process mean, shrinking Rˆt towards a fixed benchmark μ0 with oracle weight V(m)/[V(m)+(μ0−R¯)2] can give risk below vR; this lies outside the conditionally unbiased class of Proposition 1, and estimating the weight requires its own risk analysis.

B.2 Allocation between periods, cases and coverage

Proposition 3 (Budget allocation between periods and cases).

Under H1–H4, independent, identically distributed transmission periods, conditionally independent counts, fixed ρ and linear costs, let the budget be ℬ=T(c0+c1m) with c0,c1>0, and treat T≥1 and m>0 as continuous. If vR>0 and ℬ>c0, process-mean risk (c0+c1m)(vR+A/m)/ℬ is strictly convex in m and is minimised at

(B.2)

The optimum in Eq. (B.2) has the form of cluster-size allocation in survey sampling and multilevel design [12, 56]: cases per period should grow only with the square root of m× and of the relative cost of a period. Integer designs compare the risk over feasible integer T with nT=⌊(ℬ/T−c0)/(c1ρ)⌋. Under temporal dependence the variance term becomes vRS(ϕ,T)/T2 and no closed-form optimum follows.

Corollary 3 (Coverage against completeness).

Under H2–H5, let pt be the participating fraction of ν independent reporting units, each participating with probability ρ, so that τ2=(1−ρ)/(ρν). A proportional increase in completeness ρ reduces single-period process-mean risk more than the same proportional increase in exposure n exactly when m>ρ2(ν−1)/k.

Write the single-period risk as vR+vH+AH/m with vH=τ2Q, Q=R¯2+vR and m=ρn, and differentiate with respect to logρ and logn. The difference of the two derivatives is

(B.3)

Because Q/(kn)>0, the difference is negative, and a proportional increase in ρ lowers the risk more than the same increase in n, exactly when kn+ρ>ρν, that is, when m>ρ2(ν−1)/k. The mechanism is assumed; observed facility participation alone does not imply it.

B.3 Number of seasons

Suppose S≥2 season effects are independent Gaussian with unknown mean and variance vS>0, and the count law given the effects does not depend on these parameters. Any estimator unbiased for vS then has relative standard error at least (2/(S−1))1/2. Observing the effects themselves gives at least as much information as the counts, and their sample variance is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator [11, 23]. With the four seasons analysed here the bound is (2/3)1/2=0.82, and additional admissions within the same seasons leave it unchanged. This bound concerns the precision with which the between-season variance component can be estimated; it is distinct from the power of a test of equal season intercepts, which depends on the size of the season differences relative to their standard errors and is reported in Section 5.3.

B.4 Thinning and the delta approximation

The thinning check of Eq. (18) rests on a delta approximation, so its exact expectation was computed on the observed counts. For each retention probability q the expected increment of the inverse-count slope was evaluated by summing over the binomial law of every thinned count (Table S5; Fig. S1A). The exact increment rate is 0.467 at q=0.8, rises to 0.505 at q=0.3 and falls to 0.480 at q=0.2 and 0.384 at q=0.1. The least-squares rate over all q is 0.408, or 0.917 bP, against the Monte Carlo estimate 0.405 (0.366–0.441), or 0.909 (0.810–0.999) bP (Table S6).

The pooled rate is dominated by the smallest retention probability. The value q=0.1 carries 76% of the leverage in the least-squares rate (Fig. S1B), and without it the rate is 0.488, or 1.096 bP. At q=0.1 many thinned counts are small, and the delta approximation of the variance of a log thinned count fails there. At C=5 and q=0.1 the exact added variance of log(Bin(C,q)+0.5) is 0.21 of the delta value (Table S7; Fig. S1C). The positive-part truncation of the fitted mean never binds. The shortfall of the pooled rate below bP is therefore a property of the approximation at small thinned counts, not evidence about the data-generating process.

In the audit the ratio c/bP lies in 0.95–1.00 under S0, 0.96–1.04 under S4, 0.87–0.98 under S5, 0.83–0.93 under S3 and 0.81–0.92 under S6. The observed value lies outside the ranges of the generators with Poisson offspring (S0, S1, S2P and S4) and inside those with negative binomial offspring, but its confidence interval overlaps all of them. Because thinning adds known binomial variance whatever the original counting process, the check cannot separate offspring overdispersion from under-reporting.

B.5 Cross-regime check on COVID-19 counts from mainland China

The diagnostics were applied to weekly confirmed COVID-19 cases from the Johns Hopkins CSSE repository [54] for the 31 provincial-level units of mainland China. The primary period runs from 25 January 2020 to 3 December 2022, before routine mass testing ended on 7 December 2022. Hong Kong SAR and Macao SAR enter only a sensitivity analysis, and Taiwan, China is not in the extract. Rows are unit-weeks with Ct≥5 inside national growth windows. Each window starts at a national peak of at least 100 weekly cases and extends back while the national growth factor is at least 1.05. The rule does not use the growth factor of the row itself, so the selection does not depend on the regressed outcome.

The generation interval is gamma with mean 3.95 days and standard deviation 1.51 days before 2022 [57]. From 2022 the Omicron BA.1 serial interval, with mean 3.5 days and standard deviation 2.4 days, serves as a proxy [58], and bP uses the interval of each row. Negative daily increments, which occur in 30 unit-weeks, are set to zero.

The primary fit on 711 unit-weeks gave a=0.133 (0.074–0.223), b/a=13.2 (1.3–42.3) and b/bP=0.54 (0.05–2.78) (Table S16). The intercept is about nine times the influenza value. It stays between 0.119 and 0.146 for the full extract to 21 January 2023, window thresholds of 1.02 and 1.10, inclusion of the two SARs, removal of weeks with negative revisions, counts of at least 20 and the two sub-periods. Because a contains reporting variation (Proposition 2), the larger intercept is consistent both with greater variation in testing and case definitions and with greater transmission heterogeneity, and these data do not separate the two. The slope-ratio interval contains 1 and values well below it, so the panel is uninformative about counting variation relative to the Poisson reference.

Two specification choices change the results. A single interval with mean 5.2 days throughout raises a to 0.298 and b/bP to 4.62, and selecting rows on their own growth factor lowers a to 0.054 and raises b/bP to 2.18. The comparison therefore supports one conclusion. Under every outcome-independent specification with a period-specific interval, the intercept in this regime is several times larger than in US influenza hospital admissions.

The comparison has further limits. Confirmed cases in this period may include imported cases, testing regimes and case definitions changed repeatedly, and the JHU CSSE series contains batch reporting, so weekly counts mix transmission with surveillance practice. The intercept also depends strongly on the generation interval, since a single 5.2-day interval more than doubles it, from 0.133 to 0.298. The panel is therefore a sensitivity check of the diagnostics in a different reporting regime and supports no conclusion about transmission.

Affine loss with one intercept per season and a common slope (group FGLS); state-week bootstrap, 2,000 draws (1,999 valid). The season-centred column centres × on season means before forming the loss. Tests use the bootstrap covariance of the season parameters (1,995 of 2,000 draws with all parameters finite); with a common slope, equal log as is equivalent to equal season b/a. Cochran Q uses inverse-variance weights. The separate-fit test refits the loss in each season on its own bootstrap stream. For the minimum detectable difference, noncentrality 10.90 gives 80% power for a level-0.05 chi-square(3) test; scaling the observed log as deviations by f = 1.41 reaches it, which corresponds to the highest/lowest a shown. The highest to lowest season b/a ratio (2.54 [1.52, 6.01]) is descriptive and is not a homogeneity test.
